**Data Analyst, Helix Genomics Institute, Porto** — Sep 2021 to Jan 2024 (R, LI-Pos)
- Supported sequencing operations (R, LI-Pos)
- Reporting time reduced — **R says 40%, LI-Pos says 60%** (disagreement)

- Recommendation on file from Beatriz Lima, Head of the Sequencing Core: "Rafael's dashboards changed how the core plans its week. He is the reason we stopped double-booking the sequencers." (LI-Rec, 2024-02-11, visible)

**Intern, Atlantico Telecom, Porto** — R says "summer 2020"; LI-Pos says Jun 2020 to Sep 2020 (consistent)
- Churn analysis (R, LI-Pos)

**Founder, DataTugas, Porto** — Oct 2018 to Jun 2020 (LI-Pos)

## Projects

**FraudShield** — "Real-time fraud detection system" (R, LI-Proj). LI-Proj dates it Jan 2022–Jun 2022, which falls inside the Helix Genomics job (Sep 2021–Jan 2024). **AutoPilot** — "Automation platform for analytics teams" (R, LI-Proj). LI-Proj dates it Mar 2024–present, which overlaps the current Meridian Bank job (Feb 2024–present). Whether this is Meridian's project, a personal side project, or something else is not stated (gap). No URL given.

**Lisbon Rent Map** — "A map of what a room costs in every parish of Lisbon" (LI-Proj). Live at https://rentmap.example (LI-Proj). Visitor count — **R says 5,000/month, LI-Proj says 3,000/month** (disagreement). Started May 2023, no end date (LI-Proj).

## Awards

- Winner, Health Data Hackathon 2023 (R, LI-Honors), issued Nov 2023. Solo or team entry not stated (gap).

## Skills (LI-Skills)

SQL, Python, Tableau, Power BI, dbt, Statistics

## What others have said

- Beatriz Lima (Head of the Sequencing Core, Helix Genomics): see quote above (LI-Rec).

## What he learned from

- Not stated anywhere in the material (gap) — to ask.

## Pictures, drawings or files

- None mentioned in either source: no screenshots of the Meridian or Helix dashboards, no image of the Lisbon Rent Map, no photo of Rafael, no logo for DataTugas, FraudShield or AutoPilot (gap).

## Gaps

1. No picture or screenshot of any project — not the dashboards, not the Rent Map, not a personal photo.
2. DataTugas has no description anywhere — what it did, what Rafael's role was, what came of it.
3. FraudShield's relationship to the Helix Genomics job is unstated (employer's work, freelance, or personal/course project).
4. AutoPilot's relationship to the current Meridian Bank job is unstated (employer's work or side project).
5. No outcome stated for the Health Data Hackathon win beyond "winner" — solo or team, what was built.
6. What Rafael learned from (a book, a person, a first failure) is not in the material.

## Disagreements

1. Helix Genomics reporting-time reduction: resume says 40%, LinkedIn Positions says 60%.
2. Lisbon Rent Map visitors: resume says 5,000/month, LinkedIn Projects says 3,000/month.
3. MSc Data Science end year: resume says 2021, LinkedIn Education says 2022.

## To confirm

1. Helix Genomics reporting time — was it reduced by 40% or 60%? What exactly was measured (time to produce a report, time to a decision, something else), over what period, and is this your result alone or your team's?

3. MSc Data Science — did it run 2020–2021 or 2020–2022?

7. AutoPilot — is this a Meridian Bank project or something of your own? Is it in use anywhere, and can it be shown?
8. Lisbon Rent Map — is it still live and still yours to show freely, since it is public already?
9. The Journal of Genomic Methods paper — were you a named author, and what was your part in it?
10. Health Data Hackathon 2023 — solo win or a team, and what did you build?
11. Beatriz Lima's recommendation — comfortable showing her name, title and quote on the site, or would you rather anonymise or drop it?
12. Do you have any pictures to show: screenshots of the Meridian or Helix dashboards (or mockups, if the real screens can't be shown), a screenshot of the Lisbon Rent Map, a photo of yourself, anything for DataTugas/FraudShield/AutoPilot?

1	# The concept
2	
3	The second stop: from the fact sheet to three concepts the person can choose between.
4	
5	## What does not work
6	
7	- A new coat of paint on the same sections.
8	- 3D as a backdrop behind the text.
9	- One 3D scene, however good.
10	- Another site's idea with the names changed.
11	- A different effect for every section: a wall of jars, then a door that opens, then a scale that tips. Each may be good. Together they are a tour of effects, and nothing carries the visitor from the first to the last.
12	
13	## Three things to find
14	
15	**One question.** The page answers it, and the last screen gives the answer. Look where two sides of the person's work meet, or in the way from one thing to another, or in what all their projects circle. Word it as someone in HR would say it and a colleague would respect. It is about something that interests the person now, and it claims nothing the fact sheet does not hold.
16	
17	Write it as a question, with a question mark. "Teardown" and "Signal from noise" are themes: they give a page a mood. A question gives the page somewhere to go, and gives the ending a job.
18	
19	**One form.** A document or a ritual of the person's own trade that already runs from a beginning to an end, with section names a colleague would know: a paper, a runbook, a job card, a shift handover, a set of drawings. List at least five that the trade has, and take one the person said they work from. Its section names become the chapters, in its order, and no jokes are made in its voice. A chapter holds what its name says.
20	
21	"Hero, About, Work, Skills, Contact" is the form of a website. It belongs to nobody.
22	
23	**One object.** The thing that form is physically made of, in five to twelve similar pieces. The pieces carry the person's real work on their faces. They are recognisable standing together at rest. They can be built from simple shapes. They are on screen from the first screen to the last.
24	
25	The object comes from what the person makes. It is not the trade's emblem: a chef's hat, a server rack, a stethoscope. For anyone who works with data, the emblem is a field of points that gathers into a chart. It fits every analyst alive, which is what is wrong with it.
26	
27	## What every form has to hold
28	
29	Map the form's sections onto these roles. Leave out a role that has nothing to hold. Five to eight chapters. Someone with little to show yet gets a shorter story, and not a padded one.
30	
31	| Role | Holds |
32	|---|---|
33	| The opening | Their name, and the question |
34	| Who | Who is asking |
35	| Where from | The places and the years |
36	| How | The way they work |
37	| What | Some of the work shown working, then all of it |
38	| What came of it | Outcomes |
39	| What others say | Their words, one at a time |
40	| The close | The answer, and how to reach them |
41	
42	## What the object becomes
43	
44	In each chapter the same pieces take a new arrangement that shows what the chapter is about: the way they came as a line or a map, how they work as a diagram, one piece of work as an exhibit, every project as a wall whose faces carry real pictures, outcomes as cards. At the close the object is whole again.
45	
46	If a chapter's 3D could be deleted and only decoration would be lost, the pieces are not showing that chapter yet.
47	
48	**The opening shows where the object comes from.** The answer is the person's own: what they learned from, or what they began with. The object may gather, be put together, unfold, be drawn, develop or switch on.
49	
50	## Three concepts, each written like this
51	
52	Make three that differ in kind: in their form or their object, and not in their colour. Write them to `docs/story/concepts.md`.
53	
54	- **The question.**
55	- **The form,** with each chapter's name and the role it holds.
56	- **The object,** and its pieces.
57	- **What it becomes** in three of the chapters.
58	- **The opening and the close.**
59	- **What it stands on:** the lines of the fact sheet it needs.
60	- **What it needs from the person:** a picture, someone else's yes.
61	- **Why it is theirs:** one sentence on why it could not sit on a colleague's site.
62	
63	Then say which you would choose, and why.
64	
65	## Test each one before you show it
66	
67	Rework or drop one that fails.
68	
69	| Test | Ask |
70	|---|---|
71	| Swap | Could it sit unchanged on a colleague's site? Then it is not theirs yet. |
72	| Backdrop | With the 3D deleted, is meaning lost, or only decoration? |
73	| Depth | Has it a beginning, a middle and an end that follow from one another? |
74	| Emblem | Is the object the picture that stands for the job? |
75	| Honesty | Does anything in it claim more than the fact sheet? |
76	| Thirty seconds | Can someone who does not scroll get the name, the work, some proof, and how to reach them? |
77	
78	## Three cases
79	
80	How each was reasoned, and not only where it ended.
81	
82	**A research paper.** The site this skill came from belongs to someone whose work lies between AI research and software engineering. Three restyled layouts were, in their words, "all cliche". Three single 3D scenes were "not deep enough". What turned it was a sentence of theirs: "Think of it like a research question." The form became a paper, with a paper's chapters: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Method, Experiments, Results, Peer review, Conclusion. The object became the paper's nine pages, which fold into a globe for where they have lived, stand as the layers of a network for how they work, and hang as a wall of projects. The question was first too abstract for a recruiter, and was reworded. The opening was first a plain pile of pages. It became the front pages of the papers they learned from, gathering into the paper as the reader scrolls.
83	
84	**A tasting menu.** Camille is a pastry chef, made up for this page. She trained in Lyon, spent six years in the pastry sections of two restaurants, and now runs a dessert-only evening once a month: 24 seats, five courses, all sweet. People write to her about one burnt-honey tart. Her trade's forms: the recipe card, the prep list, the tasting menu, the order sheet, the costing sheet. She serves in courses and plans by the menu, so the form is a tasting menu, and each course is a chapter. Each course arrives on a plate, so the object is a stack of plates. The question: "What makes someone remember a dessert?" Turned down first: a whisk and a chef's hat turning in the air, which is the emblem, and one croissant in 3D, which is one scene.
85	
86	**An incident review.** Jun is a reliability engineer, also made up. Seven years on call, at a payments company and then at one that books hospital appointments. He wrote his team's incident review template, and gives talks on reviews without blame. His trade's forms: the runbook, the incident review, the on-call handover, the status page, the dashboard. His work is what happens after something breaks, so the form is an incident review: summary, timeline, root cause, action items. A status page is made of tiles, one to a service, so the object is those tiles. The question: "What keeps a system up at 3 a.m.?" Turned down first: a server rack turning, which is the emblem, and a globe of pings behind the text, which is a backdrop.
87	
88	**An example shows how to reason. Its concept is not taken.** Camille's menu was reasoned from how Camille serves. A chef who sells one loaf a day from a hatch is not a tasting menu. If you find one of these three concepts in your hand for someone else, it has already failed the swap test: it was made for a person who is not in front of you.
89	
90	In this version a concept is shown in words. There is no engine yet to sketch one on.

**One question.** The page answers it, and the last screen gives the answer. Look where two sides of the person's work meet, or in the way from one thing to another, or in what all their projects circle. Word it as someone in HR would say it and a colleague would respect. It is about something that interests the person now, and it claims nothing the fact sheet does not hold.

Write it as a question, with a question mark. "Teardown" and "Signal from noise" are themes: they give a page a mood. A question gives the page somewhere to go, and gives the ending a job.

**One form.** A document or a ritual of the person's own trade that already runs from a beginning to an end, with section names a colleague would know: a paper, a runbook, a job card, a shift handover, a set of drawings. List at least five that the trade has, and take one the person said they work from. Its section names become the chapters, in its order, and no jokes are made in its voice. A chapter holds what its name says.

"Hero, About, Work, Skills, Contact" is the form of a website. It belongs to nobody.

**One object.** The thing that form is physically made of, in five to twelve similar pieces. The pieces carry the person's real work on their faces. They are recognisable standing together at rest. They can be built from simple shapes. They are on screen from the first screen to the last.

The object comes from what the person makes. It is not the trade's emblem: a chef's hat, a server rack, a stethoscope. For anyone who works with data, the emblem is a field of points that gathers into a chart. It fits every analyst alive, which is what is wrong with it.

## What every form has to hold

Map the form's sections onto these roles. Leave out a role that has nothing to hold. Five to eight chapters. Someone with little to show yet gets a shorter story, and not a padded one.

| Role | Holds |
|---|---|
| The opening | Their name, and the question |
| Who | Who is asking |
| Where from | The places and the years |
| How | The way they work |
| What | Some of the work shown working, then all of it |
| What came of it | Outcomes |
| What others say | Their words, one at a time |
| The close | The answer, and how to reach them |

## What the object becomes

In each chapter the same pieces take a new arrangement that shows what the chapter is about: the way they came as a line or a map, how they work as a diagram, one piece of work as an exhibit, every project as a wall whose faces carry real pictures, outcomes as cards. At the close the object is whole again.

If a chapter's 3D could be deleted and only decoration would be lost, the pieces are not showing that chapter yet.

**The opening shows where the object comes from.** The answer is the person's own: what they learned from, or what they began with. The object may gather, be put together, unfold, be drawn, develop or switch on.

## Three concepts, each written like this

Make three that differ in kind: in their form or their object, and not in their colour. Write them to `docs/story/concepts.md`.

- **The question.**
- **The form,** with each chapter's name and the role it holds.
- **The object,** and its pieces.
- **What it becomes** in three of the chapters.
- **The opening and the close.**
- **What it stands on:** the lines of the fact sheet it needs.
- **What it needs from the person:** a picture, someone else's yes.
- **Why it is theirs:** one sentence on why it could not sit on a colleague's site.

Then say which you would choose, and why.

## Test each one before you show it

Rework or drop one that fails.

| Test | Ask |
|---|---|
| Swap | Could it sit unchanged on a colleague's site? Then it is not theirs yet. |
| Backdrop | With the 3D deleted, is meaning lost, or only decoration? |
| Depth | Has it a beginning, a middle and an end that follow from one another? |
| Emblem | Is the object the picture that stands for the job? |
| Honesty | Does anything in it claim more than the fact sheet? |
| Thirty seconds | Can someone who does not scroll get the name, the work, some proof, and how to reach them? |

## Three cases

How each was reasoned, and not only where it ended.

**A research paper.** The site this skill came from belongs to someone whose work lies between AI research and software engineering. Three restyled layouts were, in their words, "all cliche". Three single 3D scenes were "not deep enough". What turned it was a sentence of theirs: "Think of it like a research question." The form became a paper, with a paper's chapters: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Method, Experiments, Results, Peer review, Conclusion. The object became the paper's nine pages, which fold into a globe for where they have lived, stand as the layers of a network for how they work, and hang as a wall of projects. The question was first too abstract for a recruiter, and was reworded. The opening was first a plain pile of pages. It became the front pages of the papers they learned from, gathering into the paper as the reader scrolls.

**A tasting menu.** Camille is a pastry chef, made up for this page. She trained in Lyon, spent six years in the pastry sections of two restaurants, and now runs a dessert-only evening once a month: 24 seats, five courses, all sweet. People write to her about one burnt-honey tart. Her trade's forms: the recipe card, the prep list, the tasting menu, the order sheet, the costing sheet. She serves in courses and plans by the menu, so the form is a tasting menu, and each course is a chapter. Each course arrives on a plate, so the object is a stack of plates. The question: "What makes someone remember a dessert?" Turned down first: a whisk and a chef's hat turning in the air, which is the emblem, and one croissant in 3D, which is one scene.

**An incident review.** Jun is a reliability engineer, also made up. Seven years on call, at a payments company and then at one that books hospital appointments. He wrote his team's incident review template, and gives talks on reviews without blame. His trade's forms: the runbook, the incident review, the on-call handover, the status page, the dashboard. His work is what happens after something breaks, so the form is an incident review: summary, timeline, root cause, action items. A status page is made of tiles, one to a service, so the object is those tiles. The question: "What keeps a system up at 3 a.m.?" Turned down first: a server rack turning, which is the emblem, and a globe of pings behind the text, which is a backdrop.

**An example shows how to reason. Its concept is not taken.** Camille's menu was reasoned from how Camille serves. A chef who sells one loaf a day from a hatch is not a tasting menu. If you find one of these three concepts in your hand for someone else, it has already failed the swap test: it was made for a person who is not in front of you.

In this version a concept is shown in words. There is no engine yet to sketch one on.

# Concepts

Three, for Rafael Costa. He named his own daily tools unprompted: "the analysis memo (the question, the data, what I did, what I found, what I would do), the dashboard, and the weekly report." All three concepts are built from one of these three, so none of them is a guess at his trade — each is something he already said he works from.

---

## Concept 1 — The Memo

**The question.** What makes a dashboard something people actually open?

**The form** — the analysis memo, in the five parts Rafael himself named:

| Chapter | Role |
|---|---|
| The question | Opening |
| Who's asking | Who |
| The data | Where from |
| What I did | How |
| What I found | What, and some of what came of it |
| What I'd do | The close |

(Six chapters — "What others say" folds into "What I found," as a quoted line, rather than its own chapter; there's one quote on file, not enough to carry a chapter alone.)

**The object** — seven memo cards, one per real piece of work: the Atlantico churn analysis, the Helix sample tracker, the Helix weekly scheduling report, the Lisbon Rent Map, the FraudShield capstone, the Health Data Hackathon charts, AutoPilot. Simple flat rectangles, like index cards with a clipped corner. At rest they sit as one neat stack, the way a finished memo sits on a desk.

**What it becomes.**
- *The data:* the seven cards lay themselves out along a line, oldest to newest — Porto to Lisbon, DataTugas to Meridian Bank.
- *What I did:* one card — the Helix scheduling report — unfolds into its own five faces, showing the memo's anatomy worked through on a real example.
- *What I found:* all seven cards fan out into a wall, each showing its real face: the Rent Map's own screenshot, a chart from the FraudShield notebook, the hackathon's chart, a plain recreation of the Helix panel layout, and a text-only card for AutoPilot and Meridian, where nothing can be shown.

**The opening and the close.** It opens on a single blank card with just a question mark where "the question" goes — the part of the memo he always starts with. It closes on one finished card again, filled in with the site's own question, answered, and "What I'd do" written as the invitation to get in touch.

**What it stands on.** The memo structure he named; every project in the fact sheet; the Beatriz Lima quote; the Meridian confidentiality limits.

**What it needs from him.** A Rent Map screenshot. A FraudShield chart or notebook screenshot. His yes on a stylised, no-real-data recreation of the Helix panel layout (not an actual screenshot). A photo of himself, if he wants one on the opening or closing card.

**Why it's theirs.** No one else's site can open on a blank question mark and close on "what I'd do," because that order of thought — question, data, what I did, what I found, what I'd do — is the one he said, unprompted, is how he actually works.

---

## Concept 2 — The Weekly Report

**The question.** What does a week's work look like, once it's over?

**The form** — the weekly report, the other ritual he named:

| Chapter | Role |
|---|---|
| This week | Opening |
| Prepared by | Who |
| Last week | Where from |
| Method | How |
| This week's numbers | What |
| Change vs. last week | What came of it |
| Notes from the team | What others say |
| Next week | The close |

**The object** — eight analog gauges, dial-and-needle instruments built from a cylinder and a thin needle, one per real, confirmed number: Helix report time (five hours to two), Rent Map visitors (3,000 a month), AutoPilot's users (six), the hackathon team (five), DataTugas (twelve people), and three more marking years, not metrics, where a number isn't the point. At rest, they hang together like a wall of meters in a plant room.

**What it becomes.**
- *This week:* every needle rests at zero — the report hasn't been written yet.
- *This week's numbers:* each needle sweeps, one at a time, to its real reading as its project is introduced.
- *Change vs. last week:* the gauges that moved (report time, visitor count) pair up with a plain before/after, nothing claimed beyond what's confirmed.

**The opening and the close.** It opens on a stack of blank report pages, Monday's ritual about to start. It closes on the final page, signed, with "Next week" rewritten as an invitation to work together.

**What it stands on.** The same fact sheet as Concept 1, read through its confirmed numbers rather than its projects.

**What it needs from him.** The same images as Concept 1; nothing additional, since this concept leans on numbers over pictures.

**Why it's theirs.** The before/after shape — five hours to two, 3,000 a visitor floor instead of the flattering 5,000 — is the actual shape of his best outcomes, not a generic "metrics" section; the gauges only move because he gave real readings to move them to.

---

## Concept 3 — The Ticket

**The question.** How does a request turn into something people actually use?

**The form** — not one he named directly, but the shape every one of his projects already took: someone asked a question, he scoped it, built it, and it got used. This is also the language of the product-analyst job he's chasing, in a product team's own words:

| Chapter | Role |
|---|---|
| New ticket | Opening |
| Reporter | Who |
| Backlog | Where from |
| In progress | How |
| Shipped | What |
| In use | What came of it |
| Comments | What others say |
| Next sprint | The close |

**The object** — seven ticket plates, flat rounded rectangles like a kanban card, one per real ask: the Atlantico churn question, the Helix sample-tracking ask, the Helix scheduling-report ask, the Rent Map (an ask he gave himself), FraudShield (his capstone brief), the hackathon brief, AutoPilot. At rest they sit stacked in one column, unsorted, like a fresh backlog.

**What it becomes.**
- *Backlog:* the seven plates spread into a single column, oldest at the bottom.
- *In progress → Shipped:* each plate physically slides across the board, backlog to in progress to shipped, as the chapter is scrolled — the one piece of motion in the whole page that is also literally what a product analyst's work does.
- *In use:* the shipped plates pick up a real, confirmed line each — "cut the weekly report from five hours to two," "3,000 visits a month," "six people use it every week."

**The opening and the close.** It opens on one new, empty ticket with just a question mark in the title field. It closes with a "next sprint" ticket already titled with the job he's after, assigned to whoever's reading, with his contact as the only field left to fill in.

**What it stands on.** The same fact sheet; it reads every project as an ask rather than a possession, which keeps it honest about the hackathon (one ask, five people) and about AutoPilot (an internal ask at Meridian, not a public product).

**What it needs from him.** The same images as Concept 1, plus his comfort with the "ticket" framing reading as a little knowing about the product-company job search — it's honest, but it is also clearly aimed at that audience, more than the other two.

**Why it's theirs.** A kanban board is a common shape, but this one only has his seven real asks on it, each ending where it actually ended — a notebook that never ran anywhere, a script six people use, a map 3,000 people a month actually visit. Nobody else's backlog reads the same way.

---

## Which I'd choose

**Concept 1, The Memo.** It's the one most directly in his own words — he didn't just mention the memo, he gave its five parts unprompted, in that order, before I asked. That makes the opening (a blank question mark) and the close ("what I'd do," turned into an invitation) earn their place rather than being chosen for effect. Concept 3 is the sharpest pitch to the product-company audience he's targeting, and is a legitimate second choice if he wants the site to lean harder into that pivot — but a kanban board is a shape a reader has seen before, even if the cards on it are entirely his; the memo's shape is not.

| Chapter | Role |
|---|---|
| The question | Opening |
| Who's asking | Who |
| The data | Where from |
| What I did | How |
| What I found | What, and some of what came of it |
| What I'd do | The close |

(Six chapters — "What others say" folds into "What I found," as a quoted line, rather than its own chapter; there's one quote on file, not enough to carry a chapter alone.)

**The object** — seven memo cards, one per real piece of work: the Atlantico churn analysis, the Helix sample tracker, the Helix weekly scheduling report, the Lisbon Rent Map, the FraudShield capstone, the Health Data Hackathon charts, AutoPilot. Simple flat rectangles, like index cards with a clipped corner. At rest they sit as one neat stack, the way a finished memo sits on a desk.

**What it becomes.**
- *The data:* the seven cards lay themselves out along a line, oldest to newest — Porto to Lisbon, DataTugas to Meridian Bank.
- *What I did:* one card — the Helix scheduling report — unfolds into its own five faces, showing the memo's anatomy worked through on a real example.
- *What I found:* all seven cards fan out into a wall, each showing its real face: the Rent Map's own screenshot, a chart from the FraudShield notebook, the hackathon's chart, a plain recreation of the Helix panel layout, and a text-only card for AutoPilot and Meridian, where nothing can be shown.

**The opening and the close.** It opens on a single blank card with just a question mark where "the question" goes — the part of the memo he always starts with. It closes on one finished card again, filled in with the site's own question, answered, and "What I'd do" written as the invitation to get in touch.

**What it stands on.** The memo structure he named; every project in the fact sheet; the Beatriz Lima quote; the Meridian confidentiality limits.

**What it needs from him.** A Rent Map screenshot. A FraudShield chart or notebook screenshot. His yes on a stylised, no-real-data recreation of the Helix panel layout (not an actual screenshot). A photo of himself, if he wants one on the opening or closing card.

## Concept 2 — The Weekly Report

**The question.** What does a week's work look like, once it's over?

**The form** — the weekly report, the other ritual he named:

|---|---|
| This week | Opening |
| Prepared by | Who |
| Last week | Where from |
